notes.headline: Occidental: adjusted EPS of $1.91 beats by 29% and debt falls to $10 billion, clearing the way for bigger shareholder returns
notes.takeaway: Adjusted EPS from continuing operations was $1.91, far above the $1.48 consensus and $0.64 a year ago, helped by $86 oil. Occidental cut principal debt by $1.8 billion to $10.0 billion — down $10.4 billion this year — and generated $2.8 billion of free cash flow before working capital.
results: Occidental reported net income attributable to common shareholders of $1.6 billion, or $1.61 a share, for the third quarter, and adjusted income of $2.0 billion, or $1.91 a share from continuing operations; the gap mainly reflects losses on oil-price hedges. Revenue was about $6.6 billion, up from $5.5 billion a year earlier.

Production averaged 1,427,000 barrels of oil equivalent a day, above the midpoint of guidance, led by the Permian and Rockies, which offset temporary curtailments in the Gulf of America. WTI averaged $85.79 a barrel; Occidental’s realised oil price fell 11% from the second quarter to $85.91, while its domestic gas price turned positive at $1.61 per thousand cubic feet after a negative second quarter. Oil and gas pre-tax income was $2.6 billion.

Operating cash flow from continuing operations was $4.1 billion and capital spending $1.3 billion, leaving $2.8 billion of free cash flow before working capital. Midstream and marketing earned $55 million against $1.3 billion in the second quarter, as gas spreads between West Texas and the Gulf Coast narrowed, though adjusted results beat guidance.
mgmt: Chief executive Richard Jackson said reducing principal debt to $10.0 billion, after retiring $10.4 billion since the start of the year, was an important milestone. He said the stronger balance sheet allows Occidental to advance its plan to add more than $4 billion of annual sustainable cash flow by 2030, providing a pathway to accelerate capital returns.

The results reflect the sale of the OxyChem chemicals business, now reported as discontinued operations, which generated a $3.1 billion after-tax gain earlier in the year and funded much of the debt reduction.
view: For two years Occidental was a story about debt. The $12 billion purchase of CrownRock at the end of 2024 pushed borrowing above $20 billion and left the company — Warren Buffett’s largest energy holding — with little room for buybacks while its peers were returning cash hand over fist. This quarter closes that chapter. Debt of $10 billion was management’s stated target, and reaching it a year earlier than many expected, with the help of the OxyChem sale to Berkshire Hathaway, changes what Occidental can do with its cash.

The operating quarter was strong, but it is worth separating price from performance. Oil at $86 is doing much of the work, and the 29% beat partly reflects analysts using lower oil assumptions. What management controls — production above guidance at modest capital spending, and Permian well productivity — looks solid. The swing in midstream income from $1.3 billion to $55 million is a reminder that Occidental’s marketing arm can add noise in both directions, depending on gas pipeline spreads.

The investment case now shifts to capital returns and to the 2030 cash-flow plan, which relies partly on carbon capture, direct air capture and enhanced oil recovery projects whose economics depend on US tax credits. With debt down and operating cash flow running at about $4 billion a quarter at current prices, Occidental can now raise its dividend and resume meaningful buybacks; the shares at about 12 times trailing earnings suggest investors are waiting to see it happen. The obvious risk is the oil price: a fall back to the mid-$60s would cut free cash flow sharply and slow the return programme before it starts.
notes.watch: Watch the first capital-return announcement now that the debt target is met, 2027 production and spending guidance, and progress on the direct-air-capture plant in Texas and its tax-credit eligibility.
